examples: I brushed my teeth before going to bed.
I washed my hands before the meal.

Ms. Yamada went out an hour ago.
Before going out, she read the newspaper.
fields.explain:
Emphasizes the order of actions.
The tense (future, present, past …) is marked on the second verb. (V2)
The subject of the main clause takes は; the subject of the subordinate clause takes the particle が.

～まえに： Before
A length of time placed directly before まえに usually means: ~ ago.
fields.notes:
meaning_vi: Emphasizes that the action or event in the second clause takes place before the action or event in the first clause.
examples: 1. ①　つらくなる　前に
Before it becomes painful.
2. ②　テストを　はじめる　前に　名前を　書いてください。
Please write your name before starting the test.
3. ③　ねる　前に　何をし　ましたか。
What did you do when you slept?
4. ④　食事の　前に　手を　あらいます。
I wash my hands before meals.

fields.meaning: This one is more … than that one
examples: This year is busier than last year.
Trains are faster than buses.
Cats are quieter than dogs.
English is easier to speak than Japanese.
Which is more difficult, A or B? — B is more difficult.
The result was worse than expected.
fields.explain:
When the context is clear, you can say: B のほうが ～ (omitting Aより).
Add ずっと/はるかに to emphasize a large difference.
のほうが is common in conversation; formal written language may use other比較的構文, but this pattern is still standard.
Note that A and B must be compared on the same criterion.

States which is superior: “B is more ~ than A”.
The focus is on B（のほう）. The Aより part can be omitted when the comparison is implicit.
Can be used with adjectives, verbs, quantities, frequency…
のほう (the side of …) carries a nuance of choice/comparison and is natural in conversation.
fields.notes:
のほう is a nominalization meaning “side/direction”, which helps set B up naturally as the topic of the comparison.
より can become よりも for emphasis or when a clearer rhythm is needed.
が/は after のほうが: use が when giving new information, and は for contrast/generalization.
mistakes: Wrong order: “BよりAのほうが” is usually unnatural; the standard is “AよりBのほうが”.
Mixed criteria: A and B must be compared on the same criterion.
Confusing ～のほうがいい (advice) with ～より～のほうが～ (comparison of degree).
Dropping より when the context is not clear makes the sentence ambiguous in reading comprehension.

rows: A は B ほど ～ない
A is not as … as B
Focuses on the negative (A falls short of B); softer nuance than the affirmative “B is more than A”.
<ruby>私<rt>わたし</rt></ruby>は<ruby>兄<rt>あに</rt></ruby>ほど <ruby>背<rt>せ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>高<rt>たか</rt></ruby>くない。
Advice/choice, not simply a comparison of degree.
<ruby>今日<rt>きょう</rt></ruby>はタクシーのほうがいい。
Not a comparison of two sides; picks the highest degree among many.
この<ruby>店<rt>みせ</rt></ruby>が<ruby>一番<rt>いちばん</rt></ruby><ruby>安<rt>やす</rt></ruby>い。

fields.meaning: The sentence-final particle「よ」is used when giving the listener new information. The sentence-final particle「ね」is used when you want the listener to confirm information the listener already knows.
fields.connection: [sentence/clause] + よ (new information for the listener) / [sentence/clause] + ね (confirmation/empathy)
examples: Nara would be better, you know.
Oh, there's a cat!
Today's date was fun, wasn't it?
It's cold, isn't it? I want to go home soon.
Please turn there.
Please cross that bridge.
You must not run in the hallway.
I took a walk in the park yesterday.
I read manga.
I'll buy a computer.
fields.explain:
V is a verb of movement or direction, such as go, run, fly…

A
Expresses the target of an action.
B
Expresses the place someone moves through or passes.
C
Expresses the place where someone gets off a vehicle, or the starting point.
D
Expresses the state of a person or thing in the sentence pattern.

fields.name: ～を＋transitive verb＊
fields.meaning: Transitive verb: a verb that requires a complement (「～を」).
examples: I turn off the light.
I turn on the TV.
I open the door.
I close the door.
I let the cat in.
I put the cat out.

fields.name: Question word＋も（＋particle）＋～ない
fields.meaning: Expresses that there is nothing or that one does nothing (with regard to things, people, places, etc.). Used together with question words.
fields.connection: Question word + も( + particle) + Vません/～ない
examples: Because there's nothing.
I don't want to eat anything.
I didn't go anywhere yesterday.
I won't tell anyone.
fields.notes: meaning_vi: not … any ~ / no ~ at all ⏐ explain: Used to emphasize the negative. ⏐ 接続: Nも

fields.name: Noun-modifying clause
fields.meaning: How to modify a noun with a relative clause.
fields.connection: V plain form + N / Aい + N / Naな + N / Nの + N
examples: The book I bought yesterday
Please don't believe what your younger brother says.
This is a ring I got from my mother.
There are a lot of things I have to do.

fields.name: お・ご（polite prefix）
fields.meaning: お/ご: polite prefix that turns a noun into keigo (おちゃ, ご家族)
examples: Would you like to have some tea?
How many people are there in your family?
Please tell me your name.

fields.meaning: Must not do… (prohibition; spoken form of ～てはいけない)
examples: You can't smoke here, you know.
You must not use your phone during class.
Don't drink too much alcohol, OK?

fields.meaning: だ/です: to be… (affirmative auxiliary verb; だ plain, です polite)
fields.connection: Present affirmative: N・Na + だ（plain）・です（polite） / Past affirmative: だった・でした / Present negative: じゃない・ではない（plain）・じゃありません・ではありません（polite） / Past negative: じゃなかった・ではなかった・じゃありませんでした・ではありませんでした
examples: I am a student.
Mr. Tanaka is a Japanese teacher.
It was rainy yesterday.
In the class, Lin is the tallest.
Of all fruits, I like apples the best.
This is the cheapest camera.
I watched a movie with a friend.
Shall we have lunch together?
I want to go to Japan with my family.

fields.meaning: Is not… (negative of nouns/Na; じゃない is spoken language)
fields.connection: Present negative: N・Na + じゃない・ではない（plain）・じゃありません・ではありません（polite） / Past negative: じゃなかった・ではなかった・じゃありませんでした・ではありませんでした
examples: I'm not Japanese.
This is not my bag.
Yesterday wasn't a day off.
fields.notes: ※じゃありません is mostly used in conversation; ではありません is mostly used in speeches/written language

examples: I'm bad at singing.
My younger brother has poor handwriting.
I'm bad at cooking.
Lin is good at speaking Japanese.
My mother is good at cooking.
My older brother is good at drawing.

fields.connection: [sentence/clause] + な(あ)（end of a sentence, exclamation）
examples: This view is so beautiful.
It's hot today, isn't it.
I really want to go to Japan.
Dinner is ready now.
A big supermarket has opened in front of the station.
I can speak Japanese.
You can't take pictures here.
A new building has gone up in front of the station.
If you take the express, you can get there in an hour.
fields.explain:
Polite: できます／できません. Casual: できる／できない.
General ability uses Nができます; a specific action uses Vることができます or可能形V-られる.
In the meaning “be built/appear/form”, the subject is a thing + が:公園ができる,予約ができる (reservations can be made).
To show degree: よくできます (can do well), だいたいできます (can roughly do),少しできます (can do a little).

Ability/possible conditions: “can do ~”, “know how to ~” (ability, skill, conditions that allow it).
Formation/completion/coming into being: “be finished/be born/form” (a different meaning from “can”).
State the scope of ability with a noun: ピアノができます (can play the piano),料理ができます (can cook).
When expressing ability with a specific verb, Vることができます is formal; the plain form used in conversation is the V-可能形:読めます,行けます.
fields.notes:
Distinguish the two meanings “can do” and “be built/be made” based on the context and the subject.
With people:友だちができる = make a new friend;子どもができる = get pregnant/have a child (be careful with the nuance).
Places/equipment: ここで充電ができます (you can charge here) = the conditions allow it.
Polite negative in public places: 〜ことはできません/ご遠慮ください differ in nuance (prohibition/request to refrain).
explain: Expresses ability or possibility regarding something.
examples: 1. A:　カリナちゃんは　漢字が　できますか。
B:　はい、漢字をよむことが　できます。書くことも　できますよ。
A: Does Karina know kanji?
B: Yes, she can read kanji. She can write them too.
2. A:　カードで　はらうことが　できますか。
B:　はい、できますよ。
A: Can I pay by card?
B: Yes, of course.
explain: ◎ Used with the dictionary form of a verb; means it is possible to do that action.
examples: 1. 屋上から 富士山を 見る ことが できます。
You can see Mt. Fuji from the rooftop.
2. ここから 先は、車で、通る ことが できません。
Beyond this point, cars cannot pass.
explain: Vる + こと + が + できます: more polite than the potential V-られる.
Use に/で to show the place/condition:学校で勉強することができます。
Can be used both for inherent ability and for ability due to circumstances/permission.
examples: 1. 私は泳ぐことができます。
I can swim.
2. この図書館で日本語の本を読むことができます。
You can read Japanese books at this library.
3. ここでは写真を撮ることができません。
You can't take pictures here.
4. 昨日、早く帰ることができました。
Yesterday I was able to go home early.
5. このカードで払うことができますか。
Can I pay with this card?
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
Vる + ことができます | Can do (polite) | Formal, easy to use at N5 | 日本語（にほんご）を話（はな）す ことができます
V可能（かのう）形（けい） (～られる) | Can do | Concise, conversational; higher level | 日本語（にほんご）が話（はな）せる
N + ができます | Can do/know N | Used with nouns of ability | 料理（りょうり） ができます
common_mistakes: Wrong particle: ×日本語を話すができます → ✓日本語を話すことができます.
Omitting こと: ×車を運転ができます → ✓車を運転することができます or車の運転ができます.
Confusing permission and ability: rely on the context/place to understand correctly.
explain: Compared with the V-可能形: ことができる is formal/objective; the V-可能形 is more natural and colloquial:日本語が話せる。
In a nominalized clause, keep the particle order inside:日本語 を 話すことができる (correct); the pattern日本語 が 話せる is used with the potential form.
To express “service availability”: こちらで両替 できます (more natural in instructions).
Combining for emphasis:少しなら/十分に/自由に + できる.
examples: 1. 私は日本語を話すことができます。
I can speak Japanese.
2. ここではWi‑Fiを無料で利用することができます。
You can use Wi‑Fi for free here.
3. 事故のため、今日は運転することができません。
Because of the accident, I can't drive today.
4. このアプリで予約することができる。
You can make reservations with this app.
5. 手術のおかげで、また走ることができるようになった。
Thanks to the surgery, I became able to run again.
comparison: Pattern | Meaning | Difference | Short example
V-ことができる | Can (objective) | Formal; suits written language, announcements | 入場（にゅうじょう）する ことができません
V-可能（かのう）形（けい）（読（よ）める等（ひとし）） | Can (natural) | Colloquial; object changes を→が | 日本語（にほんご） が 話（はな）せる
～てもいい | Allowed to | A different axis of meaning (permission) | ここで写真（しゃしん）を撮（と）っ てもいい
Nができる | Know/be good at/be made | Noun form: 英語（えいご）ができる/ケーキができる | 彼（かれ）は数学（すうがく） ができる
common_mistakes: • Confusing permission vs ability: “入ってもいい” (allowed) ≠ “入ることができる” (able to enter).
• Wrong particle inside the clause: 日本語が話すことができる → should be 日本語を話すことができる.
• Redundancy with サ変: “予約をすることができる” is long; natural: 予約できる / 予約することができる (when formality is needed).
• Too formal in casual conversation: ことができる → use the 可能形 to sound natural.
meaning_vi: Expresses a situation in which an action can always be carried out (①②), or an ability to do something (③). Verbs expressing a person's volitional actions are usually used with this sentence pattern. It is a stiffer way of speaking than ～（され）ます。
examples: 1. ①このコンビニでは24時間買い物ができます。
You can shop 24 hours a day at this convenience store.
2. ②今、この建物の中には入ることができません。
You can't go inside this building right now.
3. ③私は日本の県の名前を全部いうことができます。
I can name all the prefectures of Japan.
meaning_vi: being able to do something…
judging from the situation, being able to do something…
examples: 1. わたしは車の運転ができます。
I can drive a car.
2. リンさんは日本語を話すことができます。
Lin can speak Japanese.
3. 「場所がどこかわかりますから、一人で行くことができます」
“I know where the place is, so I can go by myself.”
4. この図書館は9時まで利用することができます。
This library can be used until 9 o'clock.
5. 「禁煙です。ここではたばこを吸うことはできません」
“No smoking. You can't smoke here.”
6. 「このいすは壊れていますから、座ることはできません。注意してくださいね。」
“This chair is broken, so you can't sit on it. Please be careful.”
meaning_vi: Expresses that something can be done.
examples: 1. ①　何でも　食べられるよ。
I can eat anything.
2. ②　わたしは　何でも　食べる　ことが　できます。
I can eat anything.
3. ➂　いつか　また　会えますよ。
We'll be able to meet again someday.
mistakes: Wrong particle: using を instead of が for ability. Correct: Nができます.
Confusing the completion meaning: “駅ができました” does not mean “can station”, but “a new station has been built”.
Mistakenly using Nをすることができる (redundant). Usually Vることができる or Nができる is used.
Confusing degree: “少しできます/全然できません” are natural expressions of degree in the JLPT.

rows: Ability to do a specific action
<ruby>予約<rt>よやく</rt></ruby>することができる
V-<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby><ruby>形<rt>けい</rt></ruby> (<ruby>読<rt>よ</rt></ruby>める)
Emphasizes change, not simply present ability
<ruby>登録<rt>とうろく</rt></ruby>が<ruby>可能<rt>かのう</rt></ruby>だ

examples: She taught me a lot about life in Japan.
He let me know that Professor Mori's class was canceled.
My friend helped me with my homework.
My teacher corrected my pronunciation.
You lent me this book, and it really helped.
Can you wait a moment?
fields.explain:
The subject is the doer (ga/wa) + V-て + くれる; the receiver is I/we (usually omitted).
Shows gratitude and familiarity; switch to くださる when the doer requires respect.
In the request form, add a polite cushion phrase: すみませんが、～て くれますか ／～て くれませんか .
Not used to say “I do something for someone else”; in that case use ～てあげる／～てさしあげる.

• Expresses an action that “someone does (for the benefit of) the speaker or someone in the speaker's group”. Emphasizes the favor and a sense of gratitude/positive evaluation.
• Can be used to make a request in question form: ～てくれる？／～てくれますか (request).
• In emotional contexts: ～てくれてありがとう／～てくれてよかった (expressive).
• When the doer is a superior/customer, change to ～てくださる (honorific); to emphasize that the receiver is me, use ～ていただく (humble).
fields.notes:
• ～てくれるな is a blunt prohibition (don't you do it), often found in rhetoric/classical style/strongly masculine speech; use with care.
• ～てくれてよかった／～てくれてうれしい: a positive emotional nuance about the favor received.
• Changing the viewpoint: with もらう, the receiver is the subject; with くれる, the giver is the subject. Both can describe the same event with different nuances.
meaning_vi: ~smiley1V for me.
explain: Used only for yourself and your family members such as father, mother, older brother, older sister…（ちち、はは、あね、あに、おとうと、いもうと…)
私に can be omitted; in that case the subject takes the particle が.
examples: 1. A:　犬が　かわいいですね。
B:　ええ、姉が　この犬 を　買ってくれましたよ。
A: Your dog is so cute.
B: Yeah, my sister bought it for me.
2. A:　すてきな　セーターですね。
B:　ありがとう　ございます。ママが　送ってくれましたよ。
A: That's a lovely sweater.
B: Thank you. My mom sent it to me.
meaning_vi: The subject of the sentence is not the speaker. The receiver of the thing or action is the speaker or someone psychologically close to the speaker. When receiving from a superior who is not a family member, the pattern くださいます is used.
examples: 1. ①山田さんは私に時計をくれました。
Mr. Yamada gave me a watch.
2. ②先生が妹に本をくださいました。
The teacher gave my younger sister a book.
3. ③友達が店の場所を教えてくれました。
My friend told me where the shop is.
4. ④サラさんは一緒に病院へ行ってくれた。
Sarah went to the hospital with me.
mistakes: Using くれる when the receiver has no connection to the speaker → use あげる/もらう depending on the direction of the favor.
Forgetting to switch to keigo with a superior: × 先生が教えてくれた → ✓ 教えてくださいました／教えてくださった。
Mixing up くれる and もらう when the subject changes: JLPT questions often ask you to change the structure while keeping the meaning.
Using the command form くれ sounds rude; avoid it in polite settings.

rows: Someone else does something for me
<ruby>母<rt>はは</rt></ruby>が<ruby>作<rt>つく</rt></ruby>ってくれた
<ruby>先生<rt>せんせい</rt></ruby>が<ruby>教<rt>おし</rt></ruby>えてくださった
<ruby>友<rt>とも</rt></ruby>だちに<ruby>手伝<rt>てつだ</rt></ruby>ってもらった
I do something for someone else
The benefit goes from me outward

<ruby>案内<rt>あんない</rt></ruby>してさしあげます
